a: May his God be with him
p: Ezra reads 'may (his God) be' (yehi). Chronicles reads the divine name (YHWH) in the same place.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): καὶ ἔσται ὁ θεὸς αὐτοῦ μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: may his God be with him
readings.plain: May his God be with him

readings.w: 2 Chronicles 36:23 (Masoretic Text; the site's Plain English Translation); 1 Esdras 2:5 (KJV, 'let the Lord, even his Lord, be with him')
readings.en: the LORD his God be with him
readings.plain: The LORD his God be with him

why: The two words look alike in Hebrew (yhy and yhwh). Ezra's form is a wish, Chronicles' a blessing in the LORD's name. Most scholars think one was misread from the other, and the Plain English Translation keeps each book's own text. 1 Esdras seems to combine them.

a: 410 silver bowls of a second kind
p: The Hebrew 'of a second kind' (mishnim) is odd. The Greek of Ezra has 200; 1 Esdras has 2,410.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.orig: כְּפוֹרֵי כֶסֶף מִשְׁנִים אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת וַעֲשָׂרָה
readings.en: silver bowls, second (kind), four hundred and ten
readings.plain: 410 silver bowls of a second kind

readings.w: 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): ἀργυροῖ διακόσιοι, with no word for 'second kind'
1 Esdras 2:12 (KJV, 'of silver two thousand four hundred and ten'); a common modern correction of mishnim to alpayim, 'two thousand'

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. Many scholars think mishnim is a slip for alpayim, 'two thousand,' which would make the bowls 2,410 and bring the total nearer the 5,400 of 1:11. The Greek translator seems to have read the word as 'two' (hundred). See the note on 1:11.

p: The Hebrew of Ezra has 'Kiriath-arim.' Nehemiah 7:29 and the Greek read the well-known town Kiriath-jearim.

readings.w: Nehemiah 7:29 (Masoretic Text); 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): Καριαθιαριμ; 1 Esdras 5:19, as a separate line with its own number, 25: 'Kartathiarius' in Codex Vaticanus (Swete; the site's 1 Esdras), 'Kariathiarius' in Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes), which the KJV spells 'Kiriathiarius.' Next Vaticanus has 'Piras and Berog, 700' and Alexandrinus 'Caphiras and Beroth, 743' (Chephirah and Beeroth); the KJV prints both lines, 'Caphira and Beroth, 743' and 'Pira, 700'
Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) of Ezra 2:25 (KJV 'Kirjath-arim')

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from the Leningrad Codex. Kiriath-jearim, 'town of forests,' is the town where the ark stayed (1 Samuel 7:1-2) and is grouped with Chephirah and Beeroth in Joshua 9:17. Ezra's Hebrew has probably lost a letter (yod) in copying; the Greek of Ezra itself has the longer name.

p: The written Hebrew has 'Shamlai'; the Masoretes' reading, and Nehemiah 7:48, have 'Shalmai.'

readings.w: Masoretic Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud); Nehemiah 7:48
Masoretic Ketiv (the consonants as written in the Leningrad Codex)

why: The two forms differ only in the order of two letters, an easy slip. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, which agrees with the same list in Nehemiah.

t: Meunim and Nephusim, or Meinim and Nephisim?
p: In both names the written Hebrew has an i-vowel letter (yod) where the Masoretes read u (waw).

readings.w: Masoretic Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud); Nehemiah 7:52 has Meunim and a longer form of the second name
Masoretic Ketiv (the consonants as written in the Leningrad Codex)

why: Yod and waw look alike in the Hebrew script and are often confused. Meunim fits a known people (the Meunites of 1 Chronicles 4:41; 2 Chronicles 26:7), and Nehemiah supports it. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere in both names.

p: Ezra has 200 singers. Nehemiah 7:67 and 1 Esdras 5:41 have 245. A copying slip may explain either figure.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
Nehemiah 7:67 (Masoretic Text); 1 Esdras 5:41 (KJV, 'two hundred forty and five')

why: The next line gives 245 mules (2:66), and two copying slips are possible, pointing opposite ways. (1) In Nehemiah, a copyist's eye may have run from the singers' "two hundred" to the mules' "two hundred and forty-five": then Nehemiah's 245 singers are really the mules' number, Ezra's 200 is right, and Nehemiah lost its horses-and-mules line (Nehemiah 7:68). (2) Or the singers really were 245, a copyist of Nehemiah skipped from that 245 to the mules' 245, and Ezra's 200 is a separate slip or a round figure. The Plain English Translation keeps Ezra's own number; see the variants on Nehemiah 7:67–68.

p: The written Hebrew has a singular verb, 'he offered'; the Masoretes read the plural.

readings.w: Masoretic Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud)
Masoretic Ketiv (the consonants as written in the Leningrad Codex)

why: The plural fits the people as subject of the verse. The singular could mean the people as one body, or Jeshua as the priest who did the offering. The sense hardly changes; the Plain English Translation follows the Qere.

t: Sons of Judah, or of Hodaviah?
p: The Hebrew says 'the sons of Judah.' Many scholars read 'Hodaviah,' the Levite family of 2:40. The NIV does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
Modern correction based on 2:40 and Nehemiah 7:43 (followed by the NIV)

why: The names are similar in Hebrew, and 2:40 lists 'Jeshua and Kadmiel, from the line of Hodaviah' as Levites, so the correction is attractive. But 'Judah' can be kept if it means the Levites who belonged to the province of Judah. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and gives the correction here.

a: We have offered sacrifices to him
p: The written Hebrew says 'we have not sacrificed'; the Masoretes' reading, followed by almost all versions, says 'to him we have sacrificed.'

readings.w: Masoretic Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud); 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): καὶ αὐτῷ ἡμεῖς θυσιάζομεν; 1 Esdras 5:66 (KJV, 'do sacrifice unto him'); KJV and modern versions
readings.plain: We have offered sacrifices to him

readings.w: Masoretic Ketiv (the consonants as written in the Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: Yet we have not offered sacrifices

why: lo 'to him' and lo 'not' sound the same and differ by one letter. The Qere fits the sentence: the speakers say they have worshiped Israel's God for generations. The Ketiv is usually taken as a scribal slip. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere with nearly every translation. 1 Esdras 5:66 (KJV) also names the Assyrian king differently, 'Azbazareth' instead of Esarhaddon.

p: The written Hebrew has a singular, 'his colleague'; the Masoretes read the plural.

readings.w: Masoretic Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud)
Masoretic Ketiv (the consonants as written in the Leningrad Codex)

why: The singular may be a collective noun or an Aramaic-style spelling of the plural, so the two readings probably mean the same. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere.

p: The written Aramaic reads 'that is,' explaining the people of Susa. The Masoretes marked a people's name to be read instead, 'the Dehavites.'

readings.w: Masoretic Ketiv (the consonants as written in the Leningrad Codex); 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): Σουσαναχαῖοι οἵ εἰσιν Ηλαμαῖοι, 'Susanchites, who are Elamites'; most modern versions
Masoretic Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud); KJV ('the Dehavites')

why: No people called Dehavites is known elsewhere, and Susa was the capital of Elam, so 'the people of Susa, that is, the Elamites' makes good sense, and the Greek of Ezra reads it that way. The KJV followed the Masoretes' reading. Here the Plain English Translation follows the written text, not the Qere.

p: The Aramaic says 'the city' of Samaria. The Greek and most modern versions say 'the cities.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): ἐν πόλεσιν τῆς Σομορων; ESV, NIV, BSB

why: The written form is singular, but it may be read as a collective or, with a small change, as plural, which matches 2 Kings 17:24, where settlers are placed 'in Samaria's towns.' Either way the meaning is the region around Samaria.

p: Here the written Aramaic has the plural 'your servants'; the Masoretes read a singular, used as a collective.

readings.w: Masoretic Ketiv (the consonants as written in the Leningrad Codex)
Masoretic Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud)

why: Both mean the same group, the men of Beyond the River. The Plain English Translation follows the Ketiv here, because the plural reads naturally in English; with 4:9, this is one of two places in 1–6 where it does not follow a Qere.

p: The Aramaic has 'we said,' as if the narrator were one of the Jews, or as if this were Tattenai's report. The Greek has 'they said.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: then thus we said to them

readings.w: 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): τότε ταῦτα εἴποσαν αὐτοῖς; 1 Esdras 6:4 also has the officials asking; ESV, NIV

why: The first person is the harder reading and may be a trace of the source: either a Jewish eyewitness memoir or Tattenai's own letter, which uses 'we asked' in 5:9–10. The Greek smooths it into the third person. The Plain English Translation keeps the Aramaic.

a: the man he had made governor
p: The Aramaic calls Sheshbazzar governor (pechah). The Greek of Ezra calls him 'the treasure keeper over the treasury.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1 Esdras 6:17 (KJV, 'Sanabassarus the ruler')
readings.plain: the man he had made governor

readings.w: 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): τῷ θησαυροφύλακι τῷ ἐπὶ τοῦ θησαυροῦ
readings.en: the treasure keeper who was over the treasury
readings.plain: the treasurer who was over the treasury

why: The Greek may be influenced by Mithredath 'the treasurer' in 1:8. Its reading has no Hebrew or Aramaic support. The Plain English Translation keeps 'governor,' which matches the other Aramaic title in 5:3 and 6:7.

a: and its foundations are to be kept
p: The Aramaic is hard. Some read a small change: 'and burnt offerings are brought,' as the NRSV does.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, NIV
readings.en: and its foundations are retained (or raised)
readings.plain: and its foundations are to be kept

readings.w: Modern correction (followed by the NRSV), reading אֶשּׁוֹהִי, 'its fire offerings'
readings.en: and its fire offerings are brought
readings.plain: and burnt offerings are to be brought

why: The verb mesobelin means 'carried, borne' and fits offerings that are brought better than foundations that are kept. The correction changes only the vowels of one word. The Plain English Translation keeps the received text, which can mean that the old foundations should be used, or raised.

t: New timber, or one course of timber?
p: The Aramaic says 'new' (chadat). The Greek read 'one' (chad), which many versions follow.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1 Esdras 6:24 (KJV, 'one row of new wood')
readings.en: and a course of new wood

readings.w: 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): καὶ δόμος ξύλινος εἷς; ESV, NIV

why: The two words differ by one letter. 'One' matches 'three' before it and makes a neat pattern; 'new' is the harder reading. 1 Esdras seems to have both. The Plain English Translation keeps the Aramaic and supplies 'one' from the sense.

p: The Aramaic says the elders were 'building and prospering.' The Greek reads 'building, and the Levites.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): ᾠκοδομοῦσαν καὶ οἱ Λευῖται

why: The Greek seems to have misread the participle. 'Prospering' repeats the word of Tattenai's report (5:8, 'going well in their hands'), and is kept.

a: on the third day of the month of Adar
t: The third or the twenty-third of Adar?
p: The Aramaic and the Greek of Ezra say the third day. 1 Esdras and Josephus say the twenty-third.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 2 Esdras (Esdras B), the Greek translation of Ezra–Nehemiah (Rahlfs, checked on blueletterbible.org): ἕως ἡμέρας τρίτης μηνὸς Αδαρ
readings.en: until the third day of the month Adar
readings.plain: on the third day of the month of Adar

readings.w: 1 Esdras 7:5 (KJV, 'the three and twentieth day of the month Adar'); Josephus, Antiquities 11.107 (the twenty-third day, but in the ninth year of Darius, not the sixth)
readings.en: on the twenty-third day of Adar
readings.plain: on the twenty-third day of the month of Adar

why: Some scholars prefer the twenty-third, thinking that "twenty" dropped out of the Aramaic. But the shorter date has the two main witnesses. Josephus follows a 1 Esdras-type text for the day and differs from every witness on the year, so he is not independent support. The Plain English Translation follows the Aramaic and the Greek of Ezra.
